description: Rice fields, rain, and a different green. The first morning you wake up somewhere that is not where you live is worth most of what it cost to get there.
The weeks before going to the Caspian are their own good thing. Kumar, Killingsworth and Gilovich found anticipation of an experience is pleasurable in itself and, notably, unrelated to what it cost.
energy_note: The waiting is part of the thing, not a delay before it.
notes: Waiting for Merlot: anticipatory consumption of experiential and material purchases.

description: Asked years later what made the trip to the Caspian good, people name the company rather than the content. The Harvard Study of Adult Development has been producing that result for eighty-seven years.
notes: Harvard Study of Adult Development: relationship quality is the strongest single predictor of health and happiness.

aspect: What it takes to be allowed
description: Nothing but the fare and the time off.
energy_note: The only obstacle is the fare.

description: The trip to the caspian stops being an event and becomes a reference point - retold, compared against, and eventually shorthand inside one family for a whole kind of day.
energy_note: It turns into the story about it.
notes: Experiential purchases retain value through memory where material ones decay; people are markedly unwilling to trade the memory away.
